That’s the thesis behind my diagram: Standard deploys reserve capital into tokenized-stock markets and earns trading fees from their use

S-Bills are relevant because they’re designed to let any STANDARD holder earn a premium funded by reserve buybacks, without requiring a charter or additional reward emissions

But those are two links that still need to prove themselves: external revenue coming in, and meaningful value reaching holders. My diagram is explicitly a proposed model (for now 😉)

Publish your uptime, latency, and cost. Take feature requests in the open. And if you're a real product, it's fine to charge internal teams like any other customer.

Agents make this practical. They can discover services, compare them, and route around the bad ones.

tweets.text:
Every backend service should have a /feedback endpoint.

Agents are quickly becoming the heaviest users of most APIs. When one hits a missing feature or a bug, it should be able to say so right there, in a structured way. 

If the request makes sense, another agent drafts the PR and a human approves it.  Software that improves itself based on what its users actually tried to do speeds up recursive self improvement.

tweets.text:
Mario Bros was just a classic. first game i played on my NES. game with Duck Hunt and the zapper and i got the one with the Power Pad bundled in with World Class Track Meet

Zelda was the first open world exploration game i (and most other people) had ever played. so many secrets on the map that we used to scour strategy guides and discuss it with friends at school. tried bombing every wall in every dungeon

Mega Man 3 didn't invent the formula, but it basically perfected it. the graphics and soundtrack and bosses were just peak

Civilization 1 was probably the first serious strategy game i played on the family's 286 PC. Civ 2 would eventually be a big leap, but 1 was truly epic for the time. really felt like you were managing an empire and piqued my interest in places around the world

Sim City 1 on PC was an epic management simulator. it is probably still better than most city builder shovel ware on mobile app stores. had to really manage a budget to make it work

Streets of Rage 2 was the quintessential beat 'em up brawler. amazing graphics and soundtrack. one of the most fun games you could get together with your friends and just play. closet thing we had to Final Fight at home

Warcraft II was real-time strategy basically perfected, with an engaging story and characters and art style to boot. but what made this one shine was playing it with friends (modem to modem), and later with IPX over TCP/IP tools like Kali. absolutely crazy experience playing this thing on the internet with other people

Quake is probably the greatest FPS ever created. fully unlocked camera. felt like it came from the future. and running GL Quake with a Monster 3D or similar graphics card was a defining experience. rich online IRC and web communities. amazing mods like CTF and Team Fortress. no other shooter since has done what this one did for me

Diablo defined the ARPG genre. While Diablo 2 perfected it, Diablo 1 was absolutely ground breaking. i remember my first playthrough of this one more than i do many other games (and remember trading an item with someone online i met in a lobby who quickly stole my item and killed me)
